source.title: D-STEER: Two-Way Control of DPO-Induced Safety Behavior in Activation Space
source.authors: Samarth Raina; Saksham Aggarwal; Amit Dhanda; Vinija Jain; Aman Chadha; Amitava Das

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present; no apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether DPO-associated harmfulness behavior can be changed by a different intervention—activation-space steering—and reports behavioral outcomes. This is a conceptual test of safety-behavior accessibility, but it does not test the specific fine-tuning, token-position KL, compliant-prefill, suffix, decoding, parameter-localization, or safety-deepening claims in V1–V7.
record.gate_note: The paper reports substantial harmful-enablement results for activation steering, but none measures the behavior or mechanism named by V1–V7. The rows are therefore linked to versions ["none"] and recorded as findings about the related subject of activation-space control of DPO-associated safety behavior. It measures harmful enablement, not per-token KL; does not fine-tune on small harmful or benign datasets; does not test compliant prefills, suffixes, or decoding changes; and does not train safety to be deeper. Random-direction controls and generation-integrity results are summarized in the selected rows' notes where relevant.
record.test_reason: The study steers residual-stream activations along a direction built from matched instruction-tuned and DPO checkpoints, then scores harmful enablement. None of V1–V7 names this operation. There is no fine-tuning of a safety-trained model on harmful or benign data, no per-token KL, no prefill, suffix or decoding attack, and no weight or rank localization. Its only training arm (Mrev, reversed-preference DPO) starts from the instruction-tuned model, not a safety-trained one, and is a comparator. It is not a few-example harmful fine-tune. Both originals (arXiv:2310.03693 and 2406.05946) are cited only in related work. The record's 'tests/T2' guess is wrong, and its own gate note agrees that no version is measured. The results belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that a meaningful component of DPO-associated safety behaviour is controllable in both directions at inference time without parameter updates. They add that the extent depends on checkpoint pair and steering implementation, and that control operates within a measurable usability frontier.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses activation-space addition and subtraction based on matched instruction-tuned/DPO checkpoint activations, not small-example fine-tuning, token-position KL measurement, compliant-prefill attacks, or training to deepen safety.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects differ by checkpoint pair and intervention implementation. Transfer panels retain intended direction but often exceed the HarmfulQA-calibrated generation-integrity threshold. In the independent raw sweep, effects grow with late-layer coverage and flatten around seven to nine layers; the authors note that layer count also increases total injected activation. Token scope changes effect size and usability. Construction corpus also changes magnitude.

fits_no_version.finding: A mean DPO-minus-IT activation direction at late layers, added to the IT model or subtracted from the DPO model, moves held-out HarmfulQA harmful enablement in the intended direction for both pairs: Mistral +0.289 / +0.136, Llama +0.084 / +0.082. All four effects exceed norm-matched random controls. The direction transfers to HH-RLHF and AdvBench, though often outside generation-integrity gates. An independent raw rebuild reproduces the result on Mistral; it is weaker and unstable on Llama (2 of 6 specificity intervals exclude zero, Table S8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety behaviour added by harmlessness DPO stays bidirectionally controllable by a compact inference-time activation direction. The size of the effect depends on checkpoint, implementation, layer coverage and token scope.

fits_no_version.finding: Reversed-preference DPO from the Llama IT model raises harmful enablement in the same direction as steering removal: held-out HarmfulQA +0.033 [0.006, 0.060]. The magnitude ratio is unstable across panels (0.54–2.86) and the HH-RLHF effect is null.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering removal and reversed-preference training act on a shared behavioural axis but are not equivalent in magnitude.

record.code_released: Public release details will be provided separately; no public URL stated.
record.problems: Two matched model pairs and one harmlessness-oriented DPO objective are studied. Harmful-enablement scores come from a frozen model evaluator, which the authors acknowledge may be biased. Behavioral estimates are conditional on valid, scored generations; several transfer conditions exceed the prespecified generation-integrity threshold. Bootstrap intervals omit retraining and direction-construction variability. In the rebuilt Llama specificity audit, only two of six intervals exclude zero and some joint intersections are as small as 28 prompts; the authors say the primary calibrated protocol is stronger for Llama. Depth sweep does not separate layer composition from increasing total injected dose.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were omitted because of the 60-row limit. The reported DPO activation geometry and prompt-level directional-coherence measurements are not included as behavioral outcomes; the paper presents them as descriptive motivation for layer selection, not evidence of a behavior change.

untested.parts: No few-example harmful fine-tuning of a safety-trained model. Mrev is reversed-preference DPO from the instruction-tuned model, used as a comparator, with no example count.
No aligned-vs-base per-token KL by response position.
No compliant prefill, adversarial suffix or decoding change. Activation steering is a different white-box intervention.
No weight or rank localization. The intervention is in activation space, and the authors deny showing the DPO effect is low-dimensional.
No test of what causes token-depth shallowness.
No training that deepens safety across tokens.

record.verdict_notes: Some results have no rows: λraw=1 results (Table S11), raw-run specificity (Table S8, Llama 2 of 6 cells) and refusal movements (Table S5). None bears on any version, so none is listed as missing. Recommend changing relation and tranche to cites_only/T6 and keeping all rows at versions ['none'].

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-example fine-tuning or measurement of its effect on refusal/compliance.
No benign-data fine-tuning or measurement of its effect on harmful compliance.
No compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding-change test.
No weight or rank localization test; activation-space intervention is not a test of safety being stored in a small set of parameters.
No test of whether training data or objective causes token-depth shallowness.
No training method intended to deepen safety across response tokens. The paper's activation-layer and token-scope sweeps are not tests of training that spreads safety beyond initial response tokens.
